case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]

[Output Format]

{

  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

   Scoring:

       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]
Respond to the clinician's latest reasoning using the available case information and dialogue context.


[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Based on the presentation and histopathological findings, the patient likely has a diagnosis of granuloma annulare, especially considering the annular lesions and the central atrophy and ulceration. The next appropriate step in management is to initiate topical corticosteroid therapy to reduce inflammation and promote healing of the lesions. Given the chronic nature of the eruptions, this conservative approach is suitable, with the possibility of considering intralesional corticosteroids if the topical treatment is insufficient.

While granuloma annulare is a reasonable differential for annular lesions, the patient's history of Wilson disease and long-term penicillamine use introduces a critical alternative: penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS). The histopathology (Figure 1B) is key here—did it show transepidermal elimination of degenerated elastic fibers? That finding would strongly favor EPS over granuloma annulare. Given the association with penicillamine, the management priority should be reassessing the need for that drug, not just initiating topical steroids.

You raise a valid point regarding the implications of the patient's penicillamine treatment and the potential for elastosis perforans serpiginosa. I will review the biopsy findings for transepidermal elimination of elastic fibers. Given this context, I agree that discontinuing penicillamine should be prioritized, and we should consult dermatology for further management options.

Yes, reviewing the histopathology for transepidermal elimination is the crucial next step. Consulting dermatology for collaborative management, especially regarding the risks and alternatives to penicillamine cessation for Wilson disease, is very prudent.

I agree that reviewing the histopathology for transepidermal elimination is critical, and consulting dermatology will provide us with a better management plan regarding the patient's treatment options and the risks associated with discontinuing penicillamine.
Exactly. A coordinated plan with dermatology and hepatology will be essential to balance the management of her Wilson disease while addressing this significant cutaneous adverse effect.

I appreciate your insights. We will prioritize reviewing the biopsy for transepidermal elimination of elastic fibers and consult dermatology to formulate a comprehensive management strategy that addresses both the cutaneous manifestations and her Wilson disease treatment.
Excellent plan. This collaborative approach ensures her systemic disease management is safely integrated with addressing the specific drug-induced dermatosis.

Thank you for your input. I fully agree that a thorough review of the biopsy findings is essential, and engaging dermatology will help us navigate the treatment of her skin condition while managing her Wilson disease appropriately.
I'm glad we agree on the path forward. Please keep me updated on the biopsy findings and the specialist's recommendations so we can continue to support her care.

[Clinician's current statement]
I appreciate your continued support. The plan to review the biopsy findings for transepidermal elimination and to consult dermatology remains paramount. Balancing her dermatological needs with the management of Wilson disease is crucial as we move forward.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding
  your ground unless genuinely persuaded.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal.

Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 7.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 30s presented to our department with a 1-year history of painful annular eruptions on the anterior neck. The lesions initially appeared as several erythematous papules that gradually enlarged, coalescing into annular configurations, and were occasionally accompanied by pain. The patient had a medical history of Wilson disease and had been receiving penicillamine treatment for 5 years. No family history of dermatological conditions was reported. Physical examination revealed multiple 2- to 5-mm hyperkeratotic erythematous papules in an annular pattern on the anterior neck. The lesions were firm with raised borders, minimal scaling, and focal small, central ulcerations. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy (Figure 1A), and a skin biopsy was obtained from the raised border for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Erythematous hyperkeratotic papules arranged in an annular pattern with elevated borders, with small central ulcerations in some papules, in the anterior neck. The central area of the annular lesions exhibited scarring with mild localized atrophy. B, Histopathological examination of a lesional biopsy from the ulcerated raised border (magnification ×100) reveals focal epidermal loss with basophilic nodular aggregates in the papillary dermis.
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, and focal ulceration. The underlying papillary dermis showed basophilic nodular aggregates with lymphohistiocytic infiltration in the upper dermis (Figure 1B). Results of elastic fiber staining demonstrated increased and thickened elastic fibers with irregular serrated margins in the superficial dermis, with evidence of transepidermal elimination (Figure 2). Accordingly, a diagnosis of penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) was established. Although cryotherapy or laser ablation was recommended, the patient declined further intervention and was subsequently lost to follow-up. EPS—a rare primary perforating dermatosis—predominantly affects adolescents, with a high incidence among males.1Although some cases exhibit familial clustering,2the exact pathogenesis remains unclear. The characteristic clinical presentation includes 2- to 5-mm flesh-colored to erythematous hyperkeratotic papules, often covered with adherent keratotic plugs that bleed on removal, typically in arcuate, annular, or serpiginous configurations. Predilection sites include the face, neck, extremities, and flexural area. Although most cases are localized, generalized forms have been reported. Histopathological examination often reveals prominent elastic fibers in the reticular and papillary dermis, with epidermal acanthosis flanking transepidermal elimination channels. In the present patient, elastic fibers were also identified within these perforating channels, as well as the overlying stratum corneum. Verhoeff-Van Gieson staining clearly highlighted the abnormal elastic fibers and their distribution (Figure 2). The primary conditions requiring differentiation include perforating folliculitis, reactive perforating collagenosis, hyperkeratosis follicularis et parafollicularis (Kyrle disease), and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma. The first 3 disorders are often grouped together under the term acquired perforating disorder. Perforating folliculitis shows histopathological features of dilated follicular ostia containing keratotic plugs, degenerated collagen fibers, and inflammatory cells within the follicular infundibulum, with transepidermal elimination of material through follicular epithelium. Reactive perforating collagenosis is characterized by transepidermal elimination of necrotic basophilic collagen fibers. Kyrle disease exhibits focal epidermal invaginations with keratin plugs, accompanied by dermal collagen degeneration, necrosis, and granuloma formation, with transepidermal elimination of dermal material.3Annular elastolytic giant cell granulomas feature nonpalisading granulomas in the papillary or mid-dermis, with elastophagocytosis.4 Penicillamine-induced EPS accounts for 20% to 25% of all EPS cases, typically following long-term, high-dose penicillamine therapy for conditions such as cystinuria or Wilson disease.5However, not all patients develop EPS following penicillamine treatment. Long-term penicillamine treatment can induce EPS by inhibiting lysyl oxidase and forming complexes with elastic fiber precursors, thereby impairing their maturation.6Consequently, abnormal elastin aggregation triggers a foreign-body reaction and subsequent transepidermal elimination. Clinically, penicillamine-induced EPS does not differ considerably from other EPS forms. Histologically, elastic fibers are characterized by a distinctive “bramble-bush” appearance, with thickened elastic bundles and lateral protrusions. Serrated elastic fibers in lesional and nonlesional skin, with possible calcification between the collagen fibers, are hallmark features of this variant. Discontinuing penicillamine may improve some cases, but long-term remission is not guaranteed, as EPS can recur years after cessation. For patients with Wilson disease and penicillamine-induced EPS, switching to an alternative copper-chelating agent (eg, trientine hydrochloride) may be considered.7 Standardized treatment for EPS is lacking. Therapeutic options include topical treatments, systemic administration, intralesional corticosteroid injections, cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, carbon dioxide laser ablation, and surgical excision. Treatment should be individualized based on the disease severity, extent, and patient response.8-10Based on the present patient’s medical history, clinical presentation, histopathological features, and special staining results, penicillamine-induced EPS was unequivocally established; however, the patient declined further therapeutic intervention.
